title: Washing the body
hook: the Prophet's instructions to the women washing his daughter: water and lote leaves, the right side first, camphor at the end

segments.voice: Yesterday, at the deathbed, and your line: say it softly to them. Did you say the two lines again on your own? Today, the first thing done after death: the washing. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-nine.

Women are washing a young woman's body when her father comes into the room. That's how a report in Sahih al-Bukhari begins, told by one of the women, Umm 'Atiyyah. The father is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his daughter has died. He doesn't take over. He doesn't make a speech. He gives them instructions, quiet and practical, the kind you'd give someone you trust with something precious. And when they finish, he hands them something of his own.
screen: `A FATHER WALKS IN.` → `QUIET, PRACTICAL INSTRUCTIONS.` → `SOMETHING OF HIS OWN.`

segments.voice: Here's what he told them, in paraphrase from al-Bukhari. Wash her three times, or five, or more if you see the need, with water and sidr, the leaves of the lote tree. Put camphor in the last washing. Begin with her right side, and with the places washed in wudu. Then tell me when you've finished. Notice how much of that is about tenderness. The order follows the washing a person does before prayer, and some readers hear in it a last preparation, as if to stand before Allah. The lote leaves and the camphor bring cleanness and fragrance. And the count is left open, as many times as care requires. When they finished and told him, Umm 'Atiyyah says, he gave them his own waist-wrap and told them to wrap her in it, next to her body. A father's garment, the last thing she wore against her skin. That's the root of a practice that continues. The washing is called ghusl. It's done by family, or by people from the community who have learned how, usually people of the same sex as the one who died. The body is kept covered while it's washed. It's handled slowly, gently, as if the person could still feel it. Some who do this work describe it as an honor. And the person on the table can't thank them, can't return the favor, can't even know. Some say that's part of what makes it pure. Dignity, here, isn't something the dead have to earn. It's something the living give.
screen: `THREE, OR FIVE, OR MORE.` · `THE RIGHT SIDE AND THE PLACES OF WUDU.` · `HIS OWN WAIST-WRAP.` · `DIGNITY THE LIVING GIVE.`

segments.voice: The practice: think of dignity at death. Settle, and breathe. This may be tender, so go gently. Think of someone you've lost, or of the people who care for the dead in any community: nurses, washers, funeral workers. Picture careful hands, a covered body, water poured slowly. Notice the respect in that. Then ask what dignity means for the living today: someone who can't do for themselves, who can't thank you. Choose one way to honor them. If you pray, you can remember those who have died. The bell holds the time.
Washing the body. Ghusl for the one who has died: water and lote leaves, the right side first, camphor last, and the body kept covered and handled gently. Today's word.
Your line: washed with care. Today, do one thing for someone who can't thank you or repay you, and do it gently. Tomorrow, the shroud. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: After a death, Muslims wash the body (ghusl), usually by family members or trained community volunteers of the same sex, keeping it covered, washing an odd number of times with water and often lote leaves, and adding camphor at the end.

what it means: a careful washing, the right side and wudu places first, water and lote leaves, camphor last, the body kept covered.
what a scholar hears: Umm 'Atiyyah's report in al-Bukhari, the open count of three or five or more, and the Prophet's own waist-wrap.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1253 (Umm 'Atiyyah: wash her three or five times or more, with water and sidr, camphor in the last; his waist-wrap)
Sahih al-Bukhari 167 (begin with her right side and the places of wudu)

notes: Bukhari 1253 and 167 paraphrased; confirm numbers and details. The daughter is not named in the script (reports name Zaynab; some say Umm Kulthum).
The teach says the order 'mirrors' wudu 'as if preparing her one last time to stand before Allah': this is an interpretive reading; confirm or soften.

Customs described (same-sex washers, body kept covered, trained community volunteers, 'some who do this work describe it as an honor'): confirm phrasing; spouses may wash each other in several schools.
howItsDone mentions lote leaves 'often' used; confirm.

Editor: hook no longer opens 'A grieving father' (it named a feeling the report doesn't, and repeated the week's 'A ...' openings); the wudu-order reading and 'what makes it pure' now marked as some readers'.
